hints: Look at how many electron shells each ion has, cations from Period 3 lose the outer shell while sulfide keeps it.
Notice that $Na^+$ and $Mg^{2+}$ both have 10 electrons in the same arrangement, so the one with more protons will pull harder.
Put the tiny isoelectronic cations first in order of nuclear charge, then place the much larger n=3 anion last to complete the sequence.
walkthrough:
**Sort by electron shells first**

Think of ionic size as which main shell the outer electrons are in. Both $Na^+$ and $Mg^{2+}$ lose the n=3 shell and are left with n=2 only, while $S^{2-}$ keeps n=3.

$$Na^+ : 2,8 \quad Mg^{2+} : 2,8 \quad S^{2-} : 2,8,8$$

**Compare the isoelectronic pair $Na^+$ and $Mg^{2+}$**

Both have 10 electrons, so size is decided by proton pull. $Mg^{2+}$ has 12 protons versus 11 in $Na^+$, so it pulls the same electrons in closer.

$$\text{more protons + same electrons = smaller ion, so } Mg^{2+} < Na^+$$

**Place the large anion**

$S^{2-}$ has an extra full shell (n=3) and extra electron repulsion from gaining electrons, so it is far bigger than either cation. That gives smallest to largest as $Mg^{2+}$, then $Na^+$, then $S^{2-}$.

options.A: Swaps the two cations. $Na^+$ is not smaller than $Mg^{2+}$ because both are isoelectronic but Mg has one more proton, so $Mg^{2+}$ experiences greater effective nuclear charge and is smaller.
options.B: Correct order. $Mg^{2+} < Na^+$ because of higher nuclear charge on the same 10-electron arrangement, and both are much smaller than $S^{2-}$ which has its outer electrons in the larger n=3 shell.
options.C: Completely reversed. It makes the n=3 anion $S^{2-}$ smallest and the n=2 cations largest, which ignores shells. More shells always means a larger ion here.
options.D: Puts $S^{2-}$ smallest, a common trap of thinking negative charge means pulled in or that Period 3 order is simple left to right. Anions that keep the n=3 shell are much larger than cations that have lost it.
